tagline.text: The only St. Clement parish in the Philippines and Angono's diocesan shrine

children.text: Right in the heart of Angono's old town, St. Clement Church is reportedly the only parish in the Philippines with this saint as its patron, and it was declared a shrine of the Diocese of Antipolo in 2021. Around the November 23 feast day, a pagoda procession on the lake lets you see the church and Laguna de Bay in one visit.
Angono is a lakeside town in Rizal about
29 km

east of Manila, better known by its nickname, the "Art Capital of the Philippines." Many travelers come for the Blanco Family Museum or the street reliefs, but right in the middle of the old town stands a church that has watched over the community's faith and daily life for a long time. Its formal name is the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of Saint Clement, and its address is Doña Aurora Street, Poblacion Ibaba.

What makes this church special is its patron saint. According to news reports, this is the only parish in the Philippines that has St. Clement (Pope Clement I, a martyr) as its patron. Tradition says Clement was martyred by being thrown into the sea with an anchor tied to him, which is why he is shown with an anchor in art. That is how the people of Angono, who have lived off Laguna de Bay for generations, came to honor him as a patron of fishermen and sailors. Every November 23, prayers of thanks for the lake's fish and the year's blessings continue.

The records go back a long way. The Rizal provincial government's tourism page says references to a visita, chapel, or church in Angono date back to 1571 (the town's name first appears in Fray Gaspar San Andres's "Conquistas de las Islas Filipinas" of the conquest of the Philippines, it says), and that the parish itself was officially established in 1933. The town was once the Spanish-era estate known as the Hacienda de Angono, and a marker inside the church dates the founding of the estate's chaplaincy to 1751. The present building is said to have been started in the late 19th century, with the bell tower and other buildings added in the 20th, but the years differ between sources, so they are listed in the highlights below.

The most recent milestone is the shrine declaration. Bishop Francisco de Leon of Antipolo signed the decree on August 20, 2021, and the declaration Mass, postponed because of COVID-19 restrictions, was held on May 21, 2022. The church is the tenth diocesan shrine of the Diocese of Antipolo, and its first rector was installed that same day. It is also said to be listed among the Jubilee Churches for the 2025 Holy Year. For travelers, the key point is that this is not a polished tourist attraction but a neighborhood church that still holds daily Mass. If you keep that in mind, a quiet visit of an hour or two shows you a different side of Angono.

blocks.title: The Only St. Clement Parish in the Philippines

children.text: The church's biggest story is its patron saint himself. St. Clement is portrayed with an anchor, so when you look at statues or paintings of the saint inside the church, watch for the anchor shape; it helps explain how the faith of this lake town took root. Please check on your own whether the saint's image is on display and where.

blocks.title: The Shrine Declaration and the Marker

children.text: News reports say a marker inside the church commemorates the shrine's elevation, which followed the 2021 decree and the May 21, 2022 declaration Mass. The marker is said to note both the 500 years of Christianity in the Philippines and the 270th anniversary of the 1751 founding of the estate's chaplaincy, so reading it on the spot gives you the church's timeline at a glance.

Two local blogs that trace the church's history say the bell tower was built in 1930 and a large copper bell was installed in 1938. I could not confirm these years in official diocesan or heritage records, so treat them as a rough guide. The tower in front is also the easiest landmark for finding your way around Angono's old town.

Both blogs say a glorietta (a pavilion-style structure) holding a "Christ the King" statue was built in 1952. The churchyard is a good place to fit the whole building into one frame, and photos come out softest in the morning or late afternoon. Do not photograph worshippers praying from the front without permission.

Doña Aurora Street, which leads to the church, is known for wall reliefs and sculptures. You are said to find reliefs at the Poblacion Ibaba barangay hall and a statue of "Malakas and Maganda," figures from the Philippine creation myth, at the municipal hall, so this makes a good short walk before or after your church visit. Look at the reliefs without touching their surfaces.

blocks.title: The November Feast and the Lake Procession

children.text: The feast day is November 23, and the wiki-style encyclopedia entry describes a novena from November 14 to 22 and a Bisperas on the 22nd. On the 23rd, it says, a Mass with the Bishop of Antipolo is followed by a procession to the lakeshore in San Vicente, where the saint's image boards a pagoda (a decorated boat) and crosses the lake. Fish from the lake are displayed as thanks. The afternoon time shifts with the tides and weather, so be sure to check with the Angono Tourism Office or the town hall's announcements.

Angono also holds the Higantes Festival, a parade of giant papier-mâché figures. The municipality describes it as a secular celebration separate from the church feast and the lake procession, though some see it as coming from the same spirit of gratitude to the saint. If you combine the church visit and the festival on the same day, just remember that the two events run at different times.

blocks.title: The Saint's Statue at Wawa Lakeside Park

children.text: Reports say a life-size statue of St. Clement was unveiled at Wawa Lakeside Park in San Vicente on May 22, 2022, the day after the shrine declaration. Walking on from the church toward the lake shows how the town's faith and the lake are connected. Check the current location and access when you are there.
Walk in from the Doña Aurora Street side and look at the church front and bell tower first. Check the Mass schedule on the noticeboard, and if Mass is going on, sit quietly at the back.
Go inside and read, in turn, the altar, the saint's image, and the shrine declaration marker. Take photos only where it is allowed.
Look around the churchyard and glorietta, then take a short walk to the nearby barangay hall and municipal hall reliefs.
Head to the Blanco Family Museum or the lakeshore, or have lunch at a local restaurant. Check the museum's opening before you go.
I could not find a source for the Mass and opening times, so they are not listed. Check the diocese's or the church's announcements before you go.

A 2026 festival guide lists the November 23 feast-day Mass at the church at 6:00 AM, but I could not confirm it in an official diocesan or town announcement. Times can change from year to year, so check the day-of notice and claim a spot early.
After Mass, watch the procession and preparations heading toward the lakeshore in town. The decorated pagoda and the fish decorations are the main sights.
Roughly in the afternoon, the saint's image is said to cross the lake on a pagoda, and the time depends on the tides. Check with the tourism office.

After crossing the lake, the saint's image is said to land at Poblacion Ibaba, and a street procession returns to the church. The time is approximate, and the trip home will be crowded, so leave extra time.
Some notices say the lake procession is not on the official calendar, so its time is not fixed. Calling the Angono Tourism Office at (02) 661-3646 is the safest way to confirm.
Take a UV Express or jeepney toward Angono from Araneta Center Cubao or the Megamall area. One local travel blog lists about
from Cubao and about
from Megamall, while a Cubao terminal guide (updated January 2026) lists about ₱40 by jeepney and ₱35 by van, so figures differ by source.
Depending on traffic, the trip can take
1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours 30 minutes
. On fiesta days, leaving after 5:30 AM is said to double the travel time, so set out early.
You can also transfer to a jeepney at LRT-2 Antipolo or Masinag station (said to cost around
). Fares can rise during festivals, so ask before boarding.
Routes and fares change often. Tell the driver to let you off in Angono's old town and confirm it.
Follow Ortigas Avenue and the Ortigas Avenue Extension through Pasig, Cainta, and Taytay, then join Manila East Road. There are said to be no toll gates.
Parking at SM Center Angono is said to cost about
, and from there it is about
10 minutes
by tricycle to the old town.
The church and the area around Doña Aurora Street can be explored on foot. For longer distances, use a tricycle and agree on the fare before you ride.

If you only want to see the church quietly, the dry season from November to May is the most comfortable for walking. Weekday mornings are especially calm, and if you avoid Mass times, getting inside is easier.
If you want the feast-day atmosphere, November 22–23 is best. Crowds and traffic are heavy, though, so arrive early and leave plenty of time for the trip home.

Angono has a cluster of lakeside and local restaurants, but not many places to stay. Most travelers visit as a day trip from Manila or Antipolo. Check that restaurants and hotels are still open before you go.

Fish from the lake is the town's symbol, so you can try freshwater and farmed fish dishes such as kanduli, tilapia, and bangus. On the feast day, these fish are said to be displayed on the pagoda as a gesture of thanks. I could not confirm the names of long-established businesses, so none are listed.
This is still a place of active Mass. Avoid walking around and taking photos during Mass, and keep quiet.
Modest clothing that covers the shoulders and knees is recommended over shorts or sleeveless tops.
On the feast day, spots fill up from around 6:00 AM, so arrive early.
Bring cash. One report says the plaza ATM ran out of cash early on a festival day, so withdraw at SM Center first.
Public toilets are said to be scarce. Use the ones at SM Center Angono beforehand.
During the fiesta, keep your bag and phone in a waterproof bag. Some visitors report events where water is splashed.
Carry your belongings and wallet in front of you and stay alert in crowds.
Calling the Angono Tourism Office to confirm the schedule is the most reliable approach.
On November 22–23, roads and the lakeshore are very crowded and procession times may change, so check the latest announcements.
I could not confirm Mass and opening times, so check on site.
Roads and the lakeshore along the procession may be closed. The trip home can take a long time.
Notices say alcohol sales are time-limited and drinking in the street is prohibited during the festival.
Follow safety rules and marshals' instructions when boarding a pagoda or going near the lake.
Ask permission before photographing people.
An art town that includes the old town where the church stands, with galleries, museums, and street reliefs. Some sites can be reached on foot from the church, but check the distance on a local map.
A private museum showing works by Angono's best-known family of painters. Check its hours and admission before you visit.
A site known for prehistoric rock art. Access and whether it is open to visitors must be checked separately.
The big lake in front of the town, the stage for the feast-day procession and the base of the town's livelihood. You can walk around the lakeside park and pier area.
